 8   Q.      PLEASE DESCRIBE THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY.

 9   A.      I am providing testimony responding to El Paso Electric Company’s (“EPE” or “the

10           Company”) proposals for: (i) a large increase in the residential customer charge;

11           (ii) a residential low-income discount rider; and (iii) revisions to Rate No. 42, its

12           rate for separately metered electric vehicle (“EV”) charging, that would add a

13           demand charge component to the rate and establish a revised customer charge

14           framework along with significant increases in the customer charge. 3

15   Q.      PLEASE DESCRIBE HOW YOUR TESTIMONY IS ORGANIZED.

16   A.      In Section II of my testimony, I demonstrate how the Company has overstated its

17           customer-related costs in several ways, which in turn significantly overstates the

18           supposed “cost-based” rate underlying the proposed residential customer charge.

19           Subsection A provides background information on the Company’s residential

20           customer charge proposal and the factors driving the Company’s calculations. In

 4           and as a whole undermine the documented success of the rate at encouraging

 5           flexible EV charging load.

 7           42 of incentivizing the concentration of EV charging in the super off-peak and

 8           off-peak periods.

10           charge customers for costs caused by usage during peak periods based on

11           demands that occur primarily during off-peak and super off-peak periods.

16        problematic features of the Company’s proposal that are unique to Rate No. 42

17        (e.g., service drop and meter reading costs), and how the proposed revised customer

 4        Company’s AMS system as customer-related costs, (ii) exclude certain expenses

 5        that EPE erroneously classified as customer-related, and (iii) remove the residential

 6        customer charge adder that EPE applied to recover foregone customer charge

 4   A.   At a basic level, AMS meters have enhanced capabilities compared to non-AMS

 5        meters, but those capabilities come at a higher cost. The capabilities include

 6        facilitating demand and energy savings through advanced rate designs, identifying

 7        and preventing energy theft, supporting distribution planning and distribution

 9        advanced metering that extend beyond the basic metering function, EPE continues

10        to classify metering costs as exclusively customer-related rather than using a multi-

17        reflected in the Company’s COSS.

 4          B.      EPE’s Proposal Misclassifies Numerous Costs as Customer-Related

 5   Q.      WHAT ARE CUSTOMER-RELATED COSTS?

 6   A.      Customer-related costs are costs that vary primarily in proportion to the number of

 7           customers that take service from a utility. It is commonly accepted that customer-

 8           related costs include costs for connecting customers to the distribution system (i.e.,

 9           service drops), metering usage, billing, and customer service. 8 However, within this

10           general framework, proper identification of customer-related costs should consider

11           the specific cost-causation attributes associated with individual costs within these

12           broad categories. Such a nuanced consideration is necessary to avoid an outcome

13           where the customer-related category does not become an effective “dumping

14           ground” for costs that have an identifiable multi-factor cost causation character, or

15           which otherwise do not fit clearly within a single one of the three classification

16           categories (i.e., customer, demand, and energy).

17                    (I) Appropriate Classification and Treatment of AMS Costs
